content.text:
Honest answer: **fly.io would likely be cheaper and simpler than CF Containers** for this workload, and either container path would let you skip the Workers porting effort entirely — but you'd lose the "magic" of the work you just did.

**Cost comparison (rough, late-2025 pricing for a realistic always-on instance):**

| Option | Cost ballpark | Cold start | Scale-to-zero |
|--------|--------------|------------|---------------|
| Workers-native (current) | $0–5/mo at low traffic; pay-per-request | <1ms | Yes, true |
| Fly.io (shared-cpu-1x, 512MB) | ~$3–5/mo idle, ~$10–15/mo with light traffic | ~300ms | Yes |
| CF Containers (256MB, 0.0625 vCPU) | ~$8–15/mo minimum even idle | ~2–5s | Limited (10min min runtime billing in some configs) |

CF Containers' pricing is structured for "long-running services that need DO/Workers integration," not for "I want a cheap Node container." Per-CPU-second they're 5–10× more expensive than fly.io for the same compute.

**The real architecture question is what you're optimizing for:**

- **"One-click deploy, dirt cheap, edge-distributed"** → Workers-native (what you've built). Best for the public "Deploy to Cloudflare" button story since CF pays for resource provisioning during the deploy flow.
- **"Self-host, no code changes, predictable billing"** → fly.io with the existing Dockerfile. ~10 minutes of work, no Worker porting, has built-in Postgres so you skip Neon entirely.
- **"Already all-in on Cloudflare"** → CF Containers. Only makes sense if you specifically need DO/Workers→Container routing in the same account.

My recommendation: **keep both paths**. The Workers-native deploy is the unique selling point (genuinely one-click, scales to zero, free for hobbyists). Add a fly.io section to the README as the "self-host" alternative for people who want the full Node feature set without the sidecar dance. Don't bother with CF Containers — it gives you the worst of both worlds (container costs + CF lock-in).
